description: Équipe de 5 étudiants passionnés basés à Douala, Cameroun. Nous aimons transformer les données en outils utiles pour nos communautés. Nos compétences : Python, analyse de données, développement web, design et storytelling. Intéressés par l'observation de la Terre, les satellites et les solutions à impact réel.
summary:
Dancing with the SARs : High-level summary

FloodScope uses radar and other space data to see, explain, forecast and project floods in Cameroon. In the Far North, where floods last weeks, NISAR and Sentinel-1 radar map the Logone flood; our map matches the official Copernicus emergency map with 75% precision. In Douala, where flash floods last only hours and fall between satellite passes, we use NASA rainfall (GPM IMERG), terrain and population data to score the flood exposure of 92 neighbourhoods, forecast the risk 72 hours ahead, and show who will live below high tide by 2050 and 2100. 1.16 million Douala residents live less than 2 m above a stream: FloodScope gives them, their city council and relief agencies neighbourhood-level information before the water comes.
Link to project demo : un seul lien, la vidéo de 30 s ou le PDF des 7 diapositives en accès public.
details:
FloodScope is a web application with four modules:

1. Observe (Far North, Yagoua): a before/after radar comparator of the Logone flood. Water is detected automatically from OPERA RTC-S1 (Sentinel-1) and NISAR L-band images, and compared with the official Copernicus EMS map (precision 75%, recall 56%, F1 0.64, October 2024).

2. Understand (Douala): an exposure score for 92 neighbourhoods, learned from 45 documented flood reports (press, OCHA). Each neighbourhood sheet shows what drives its score: people living less than 2 m above a stream, buildings in flow paths, drains, density.

3. Forecast (Douala): a 72-hour flood risk level per neighbourhood (+24, +48, +72 h), combining forecast rain (Open-Meteo, bias-corrected with GPM IMERG), harmonic tide prediction, soil saturation (rain of the previous 5 days) and neighbourhood exposure. Each level comes with its explanation.

4. Project (Douala): low-lying areas connected to the estuary that will lie below the highest tide in 2030, 2050, 2070 and 2100, under two IPCC scenarios, with the population concerned.

How it works?

A Python pipeline downloads open data, puts everything on a common 30 m grid, detects water (Otsu thresholding and change detection on Sentinel-1; HH darkening and the HH/HV double-bounce signature on NISAR for water under vegetation), trains a logistic regression validated on neighbourhoods never seen in training (AUC 0.757), and produces quality-controlled files (645 automatic checks). A FastAPI and PostgreSQL/PostGIS server loads them with all-or-nothing checks; a React and MapLibre application displays them in English and French. Flood reports must be verified by a second team member before they are shown publicly.

Why it matters?

Existing tools in Cameroon are regional (ONACC 10-day bulletins), river-based (Douala council river gauges, Google Flood Hub) or come after the event (Copernicus emergency maps). FloodScope adds neighbourhood scale, anticipation of flash floods driven by rain and tide, and an automatic, verified radar flood map. It complements these systems.

Intended impact

Residents can check their neighbourhood's risk 72 hours ahead. The city council gets an objective priority list for drain clearing: the 10 most exposed neighbourhoods have 613,000 residents. Relief agencies get a flood map and a forecast. Planners see that the population below high tide is multiplied by 9.5 by 2100 under high emissions.

Limits we state openly

The forecast is experimental (6 of 9 documented floods recovered at least "moderate" on held-out episodes). Neighbourhood boundaries are approximated from OpenStreetMap. The terrain model is accurate to about 1 m. NISAR 2026 results are a cross-check with Sentinel-1, not yet a validation, because no official 2026 map exists.

Tools

Python (rasterio, geopandas, scikit-learn), PostgreSQL/PostGIS, FastAPI, React, TypeScript, MapLibre GL, Docker.

References

- Otsu, N. (1979). A threshold selection method from gray-level histograms. IEEE Trans. Systems, Man, and Cybernetics.

- Hess, L., Melack, J., Simonett, D. (1990). Radar detection of flooding beneath the forest canopy. Int. J. Remote Sensing.

- Rennó, C. et al. (2008). HAND, a new terrain descriptor. Remote Sensing of Environment.

- Fox-Kemper, B. et al. (2021). Ocean, Cryosphere and Sea Level Change. IPCC AR6 WG1, chapter 9.

- Ngongo et al. (2017). Floods in the Douala metropolis. J. Environmental Planning and Management.
